groups.when: The ask opens with What is, What do you understand by, or State. It wants the thing named and bounded in a sentence or two, not a description of how it is used.

papers.quote: i) What is pipelining? 2mks

asks.answer:
Pipelining is an implementation technique in which the execution of an instruction is split into a fixed sequence of stages, each with its own hardware, so that several instructions occupy different stages at the same instant. The classic five stage pipeline is fetch, decode, execute, memory and write back.

It does not make one instruction finish sooner, it raises how many finish per unit time. Once the pipeline is full, a k stage pipeline completes one instruction every clock cycle, so n instructions take (k + n − 1) cycles instead of n × k.

papers.quote: i) What do you understand by Von Neumann Concept? 1mk

asks.answer: The Von Neumann concept, also called the stored program concept, is that a computer keeps its program and its data together in the same memory, and runs the program by fetching those instructions from that memory and obeying them one after another.

papers.quote: i) State Amdahl's law' 2mks
i) State Amdahl's law' 2½mks

asks.answer:
Amdahl's law states that the overall speedup a system gains by improving one of its parts is limited by the fraction of the total time that part is actually in use.

With f the fraction of the time that is sped up and s the speedup of that part:

S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s)

The part left untouched sets the ceiling: even making the improved part infinitely fast leaves S no greater than 1 / (1 − f). A cache ten times faster than memory, hit 85% of the time, gives 1 / (0.15 + 0.085) = 4.26, not 10.

papers.quote: ii) What happens when there is a Cache Miss? 1½ mks

asks.answer:
On a cache miss the word the CPU asked for is not in the cache, so:

  1. the cache signals the miss and the CPU stalls;
  2. the address is passed out to main memory;
  3. main memory returns the whole block that contains the word, not the word alone, because of spatial locality;
  4. that block is written into a cache line, a line being evicted first if none is free, chosen by the replacement policy such as LRU;
  5. the tag and valid bit are set and the word is delivered to the CPU, so the next access to that block hits.

The time those steps cost is the miss penalty, which is why a miss rate of a few per cent still dominates the average access time.

papers.quote: ii) What do you understand by Overflow and Underflow in data representation? Give one example for each. 3mks

asks.answer:
Overflow is a result too large for the number of bits available, so the value stored is not the value computed. Example: 8 bit two's complement holds −128 to +127, so 100 + 50 = 150 overflows, and the bits stored, 1001 0110, read back as −106.

Underflow is a result too small for the representation to hold. For integers that is a value below the most negative one storable: −100 − 50 = −150 underflows that same 8 bit range. In floating point it is a value so close to zero that the exponent cannot go low enough, so it rounds away to zero: 10−40 underflows IEEE 754 single precision, whose smallest normalised magnitude is about 1.18 × 10−38.

Both are range errors, one off the top of the range and one off the bottom.

papers.quote: ii) Mention any 2 significant aspects of Von Neumann Architecture. 2mks

asks.answer:
• A single shared memory. Instructions and data are held in the same memory and travel over the same bus, so nothing but the way the machine uses a word tells an instruction from a datum.
  • Sequential execution of a stored program. The program counter holds the address of the next instruction, and instructions are fetched and obeyed one at a time, in order, until a branch changes the counter.

papers.quote: iii) State one advantage and one disadvantage of each method. 8mks

asks.answer:
MappingAdvantageDisadvantage
DirectSimplest and fastest lookup: a block can be in exactly one line, so one tag comparison decides the hitTwo blocks that map to the same line evict each other however empty the rest of the cache is, which is a conflict miss
Fully associativeA block may sit in any line, so there are no conflict misses at allEvery line's tag must be compared at once, needing a comparator per line and a replacement policy, so it is costly and the hit time grows with the cache
Set associative, k wayThe compromise: nearly all conflict misses go for only k comparisons per accessMore complex than direct mapping, and blocks competing for one set can still evict one another

groups.when: A name on its own is not an explanation. Say what the thing is, then why it holds or what the machine does about it, and where the ask says illustrate, the illustration carries its own marks.

papers.quote: Explain the following terms 3mks i. Locality of reference ii. Temporal locality
i) Explain the following terms: 4½mks 1. Locality of reference 2. Temporal locality 3. Special Locality
Explain the following 4½mks i) Locality of reference ii) Temporal locality iii) Spacial Locality

asks.answer:
Locality of reference is the tendency of a program to use a small and predictable set of memory locations during any short period, a consequence of loops, of arrays and of subroutines. It is the reason a small fast cache can satisfy most accesses, and so the reason a memory hierarchy works at all.

Temporal locality, locality in time: a location used now is likely to be used again soon, as with a loop counter or the instructions of the loop body. The machine exploits it by keeping recently used blocks in the cache.

Spatial locality, locality in space: locations near one just used are likely to be used next, as when stepping through an array or running straight line code. The machine exploits it by fetching a whole block of neighbouring words on every miss.

Where the paper prints "Special Locality" or "Spacial Locality", the term meant is spatial locality.

papers.quote: i) Describe how cache memory improves the performance of a computer system. 2mks

asks.answer:
Cache is a small, very fast memory between the CPU and main memory, holding copies of the blocks in current use. Because programs show locality of reference most requests are found there and are served at cache speed instead of main memory speed, so the processor spends far less time stalled waiting on memory.

The gain is in the average access time, AMAT = Tc + (1 − h) × Tm. With a hit rate h = 0.96, a 2 ns cache and an 80 ns memory, the average access is 2 + 0.04 × 80 = 5.2 ns rather than 80 ns, about fifteen times faster, and no program had to be rewritten to get it.

papers.quote: iii) Describe the Von Neumann architecture bottleneck. 2mks

asks.answer:
In the Von Neumann design instructions and data share one memory and one bus, so only one of them can be in transit at a time: the processor cannot fetch an instruction and read or write that instruction's data in the same instant, and the two must take turns on the single path.

That shared path, not the processor, then sets the speed of the machine. However fast the CPU is made it spends its time waiting on the one bus, and that gap between processor speed and memory bandwidth is the Von Neumann bottleneck. It is why the Harvard design separates the two memories, and why caches exist.

papers.quote: i) Describe three (3) categories of Instructions that we have. Give two (2) examples for each. 4½mks

asks.answer:
• Data transfer. Move a value between registers, memory and input or output without changing it. Examples: LOAD and STORE (also MOVE, PUSH, POP).
  • Arithmetic and logic, also called data processing. Compute a new value from operands held in registers or memory, setting the condition flags. Examples: ADD and AND (also SUB, MUL, OR, NOT and the shifts).
  • Control transfer, also called program control. Change which instruction runs next, conditionally or not, so a program can test and repeat. Examples: JUMP and BEQ (also CALL and RETURN).

papers.quote: ii) Discuss the characteristics of computer memory based on Access Methods. Give one example for each method. 4mks

asks.answer:
• Sequential access. Records are read in the order they were written, passing over everything in between, so the access time depends on where the item sits and where the mechanism is now. Example: magnetic tape.
  • Direct access. Each block has its own address that the mechanism moves to, then a short sequential search finds the item within the block, so access times vary but only a little. Example: a magnetic disk.
  • Random access. Every location has its own addressing circuitry and is reached in the same time as any other, whatever the order of access. Example: semiconductor main memory, RAM.
  • Associative access. A word is found by its contents rather than by its address: a pattern is presented and every location compares itself with it at once. Example: the tag memory of a cache.

papers.quote: i) Describe End-Around Carry in 1's Complement? Illustrate this using 153 – 142 in a 10-bit register. 4mks
ii) Describe End-Around Carry in 1's Complement? Illustrate this using 153 – 142 in an 10-bit register. 4mks

asks.answer:
What it is. In one's complement arithmetic a − b is done as a + (−b), where −b is b with every bit inverted. If that addition produces a carry out of the most significant bit the carry is not thrown away: it is brought round and added into the least significant bit, and that step is the end around carry. It is needed because one's complement has two representations of zero, so without it every such sum comes out one short. The carry out also tells you the result is positive; no carry out means the result is negative and already in one's complement form.

153 − 142 in a 10 bit register.

153 = 00 1001 1001
142 = 00 1000 1110, so −142 = 11 0111 0001 (every bit inverted)

Add them:
  00 1001 1001
+ 11 0111 0001
= 1 00 0000 1010, with a carry out of the tenth bit

End around carry: 00 0000 1010 + 1 = 00 0000 1011 = 11, leading bit 0 so positive, and 153 − 142 = 11. Correct.

papers.quote: i) Describe the three types of data hazards. 1½mks

asks.answer:
• RAW, read after write, a true dependency: an instruction needs an operand an earlier instruction has not yet written, so it waits or is handed the value by forwarding. MUL R2,R0,R1 then ADD R4,R2,R3 is RAW on R2.
  • WAR, write after read, an anti dependency: a later instruction would write a register an earlier one has not yet read, so reordering them would make the earlier one read the wrong value.
  • WAW, write after write, an output dependency: two instructions write the same register, and completing out of order would leave the wrong value behind.

RAW is a genuine flow of data and can only be hidden, by forwarding. WAR and WAW are name dependencies and disappear altogether if the registers are renamed.

asks.context: on the segment printed with the question: LW R1,0(R2) then ADD R3,R1,R4, SUB R5,R3,R6, SW R5,8(R2), BEQ R5,R0,LABEL and MUL R7,R5,R8, with forwarding available, the branch resolved in EX, one stall per load use, a three cycle multiply and separate instruction and data caches

papers.quote: i) Identify and explain every pipeline hazard. 5mks

asks.answer:
Take each instruction's destination register and look for it among the source registers of those behind it. That, not the mnemonic, is what finds every hazard.

Data hazards, all of them RAW:

  • I1 to I2, a load use hazard. I2 needs R1, which the load only has after its MEM stage, so even with forwarding I2 must stall one cycle. This is the one RAW that forwarding cannot remove.
  • I2 to I3 on R3, and I3 to I4, I3 to I5 and I3 to I6 on R5, are ordinary RAW hazards between arithmetic instructions, and forwarding from EX to EX hides every one of them at no cost.

Control hazard. I5, the BEQ, is not resolved until its EX stage, so whatever is fetched behind it is fetched before the outcome is known. Without prediction a taken branch costs two cycles; the segment as printed is counted as falling through.

Structural hazards. The usual one, an instruction fetch clashing with a data access in the same cycle, is removed by the separate instruction and data caches the question grants. The multiplier is the one that remains: I6 holds the single execute unit for three cycles, so anything behind it would have to wait for the unit rather than for data.

No WAR or WAW hazard arises here, because this pipeline writes back in order and each of R1, R3, R5 and R7 is written by exactly one instruction.

groups.when: Differentiate or compare. Two columns and one property a row, so the contrast is visible without being read, and where a diagram is asked for it carries marks of its own.

papers.quote: i) Computer Systems are designed using two closely related but distinct concepts which are Computer Architecture and Computer Organization. Differentiate between these concepts. 2mks

asks.answer:
Computer architecture is the functional design and logical structure of the system as the programmer sees it: the instruction set, the data types, the addressing modes and the register organization. It answers what the computer does, and is the specification a machine is built to.

Computer organization is the operational units and their interconnection that realise that architecture: the control signals, the buses and their widths, the memory technology, the caches and how the units are pipelined. It answers how the computer does it.

ArchitectureOrganization
Question it answersWhat does it doHow is it done
Who sees itThe programmer, through the instruction setThe hardware designer, and it is hidden from the program
How often it changesRarely, because software depends on itFreely, between models of one family
A likenessThe architect's drawing of a buildingThe materials and methods it is actually built with

One architecture can have many organizations: every x86 processor from the 8086 onwards runs the same instruction set with an entirely different internal design.

papers.quote: v) Explain why the speedup differs from the theoretical maximum. 1mk

asks.answer: The theoretical maximum for a five stage pipeline is 5, and it assumes perfectly balanced stages, no overhead between them, and one instruction completing every cycle. This processor meets none of those: the stages are 5, 4, 6, 5 and 4 ns so the clock is set by the slowest, the pipeline register overhead adds 1 ns to every cycle, and branches (two extra cycles), floating point (three cycles in EX) and the 10% of memory accesses that miss (four extra cycles) lift the actual CPI to 2.44 instead of 1. The speedup comes out near 1.46, not 5.

papers.quote: v) Discuss how increasing associativity beyond four ways might affect performance. 2mks

asks.answer:
Raising the associativity removes conflict misses, because more blocks that map to the same set can be held at once. The gain falls away quickly, though: most conflicts have already gone by four ways, so eight or sixteen buys very little further hit rate.

The costs keep rising in a straight line. Every extra way is another tag comparator working in parallel and a wider multiplexer on the data path, so the hit time and the power both grow; LRU replacement over more ways is harder to implement; and each doubling of the ways halves the number of sets, so a set index bit moves into the tag and the tag directory grows. Past four ways the added hit time can cost more than the misses it saves, and the average access time gets worse rather than better. A fully associative cache is the limit of this, which is why only small structures such as a TLB are built that way.

papers.quote: iv) Explain why fully associative mapping eliminates conflict misses but introduces another performance challenge. 1½mks

asks.answer:
A block may be placed in any line, so no two addresses are ever forced to compete for one line: conflict misses vanish and only compulsory and capacity misses remain.

The cost is the search. With no index field to point at one line, the address tag must be compared against every line's tag, and doing that in one cycle needs a comparator per line, that is content addressable memory. So the hardware and the power grow with the cache, the hit time grows with it, the tag field itself is longer because the index bits are gone, and a replacement policy such as LRU must now be implemented and updated on every access. That is why real caches are set associative: nearly all of the gain for a small fraction of the cost.

papers.quote: iv) Suggest any two hardware improvements that would reduce stalls. 1mk

asks.answer:
• Fuller forwarding, or bypass, paths, including MEM to EX, so a value reaches the instruction behind it in the cycle it is produced instead of after write back.
  • Pipeline or duplicate the multiplier, so a three cycle multiply no longer holds the single execute unit and the instructions behind it do not wait for it.

Branch prediction with a branch target buffer, which removes the control stall on the BEQ, and separate instruction and data caches, which this question already grants, are the other two that earn the mark.
